newsitem.title: USA: Karnal bunt-like spores found on imported ryegrass.
newsitem.headline: Karnal bunt-like spores found on imported ryegrass.

text.p: Recent tests on imported ryegrass seed, even some dating back to 1967, found they carried fungus spores similar to the Karnal bunt fungus which attacks wheat, said an Oregon agriculture official.

This evidence, plus findings these spores have been present on Oregon ryegrass since 1989, support arguments ryegrass spores do not cause Karnal bunt in wheat, said Dan Hilburn, plant division administrator for Oregon's Department of Agriculture.
"If it is a Karnal bunt, it is not a variety that affects wheat," said Hilburn.

Hilburn said tests by the U.S. Agriculture Department showed ryegrass from Australia contained the spores, but Australia's wheat has never contracted the fungus. Also, he said Oregon's wheat has been free of Karnal bunt.
Oregon exports ryegrass throughout the United States including to the wheat states of Kansas and North Dakota, which do not have Karnal bunt in their wheat, said Hilburn.
Arizona officials are not convinced. To protect its wheat, Arizona requires that Oregon ryegrass seed be free of the spores before entering the state.

"Does it make any sense that we remain under quarantine (for wheat) and we allow it into the state?," said Ken Boyd, associate director of the Arizona Department of Agriculture plant industry division.

Also, Boyd said the Karnal bunt spores have been found on Oregon barley imported by Arizona. Barley is not a Karnal bunt host, but Boyd said the barley may have come into contact with the fungus during cleaning by machines that also clean wheat.
Karnal bunt was found in several states last year, including Arizona, and Arizona's wheat remains under quarantine.
Oregon's ryegrass seed is planted to golf courses, athletic fields and lawns.

Karnal bunt does not pose a health risk to consumers, but can affect the taste and smell of wheat and wheat products. Because it does not pose a health risk, Boyd said Arizona officials believe restrictions on Karnal bunt should be lifted. Also, he said wheat with karnal bunt can be blended with clean wheat to remove the adverse taste and odor.
USDA in January began testing the Oregon ryegrass spores to determine if they are the same as those found on wheat, but a USDA official said the "tests are still in progress."
